items.summaryJa: Anthropicは Claude Sheets、Claude Whiteboards、Claude Data をベータ/一般提供へ移行。Sheetsは共同編集機能を持ち、データはCSV/Excel/Google Sheetsから取り込み、書き出しも可能だが、ピボットテーブルやマクロは未対応。Whiteboardsはボード上での共同作業や文書・スライド化ができ、Dataはデータウェアハウス接続やダッシュボード作成、ストーリー動画下書きなどに対応する。外部アプリの編集画面は Claude 内だけでなく、横並びや全画面表示で開け、Adobeや Atlassian などの対応アプリを直接操作可能になる予定。なお、機能はプランや環境で有効/デフォルト設定が異なる。

items.title: Responsive design is more than resizing a window
items.summary: 🚀 Frontend Focus #​766 — November 11, 2026 | Read on the web Beyond the Viewport: Introducing Site Seeing — Making a design responsive means tackling more than just resizing, with real users often having on-screen keyboards, split views, docked DevTools, and other things open, or even using oddly sized in-app browsers. Ahmad's new, free browser-based tool is designed to preview your layouts in these awkward contexts. Ahmad Shadeed Run AI Coding Models on Your Own Machine — Local models are now good enough for everyday coding. Learn to run them on your own Mac or GPU, wire them into your editor and terminal agents, and keep your code private with no per-token bill. Master.dev sponsor 🤖 Modern Web Guidance 1.0: Web Expertise for AI Agents — Coding agents can write good code, but tend to fall behind on Web standards and best practices. Chrome's skills for steering agents toward modern, Baseline-aware HTML/CSS are now stable, and it's not just Google: Lea Verou, Patrick Brosset (Edge), and Jake Archibald (Firefox) are among the project's owners. Philip Walton (Google) The Web is More Than Enough — An encouraging reminder of the immense power of the Web platform and how advanced use of WebAssembly, Web Crypto, WebGL, and Web Audio is increasingly within the reach of developers to build apps you'd once never have imagined in the browser. Paul Ford ⚡️ IN BRIEF 🗳️ The State of JS survey for 2026 is open now and seeking responses . 🦊 Firefox 160 is now stable. On-device speech recognition via the Web Speech API arrives on desktop, and you can experiment with blocking="render" and lazy loading for video and audio behind flags. ♿ GitHub now recognizes an ACCESSIBILITY.md file and surfaces it on a repository's overview page. 🦓 Zigzag is a new lightweight browser for macOS , coming in at just 18MB. 📙 Articles, Opinions & Tutorials Computing with CSS Layout — How much can CSS 'compute' on its own? Leaning on the behavior of CSS grid, flexbox, and more, this interactive piece shows how to read CSS's 'calculations' back as numbers and put them to practical use, including drawing animated charts. Agustin Capeletto System Colors Need to Work Together — You might expect paired CSS system colors like HighlightText and Highlight to be readable together, but in Chrome on Android's dark mode they manage a contrast ratio of only 1.98:1. Aaron's cross-browser study shows which pairs hold up. Aaron Gustafson How to Build Your Own Automated Debugging Workflow — Connect your coding agent to Sentry and turn errors into fix PRs. See the guides and recipes in the resource hub. Sentry sponsor Is 'Using Declarations Just Once' Still Effective in CSS? — This classic optimization technique merges repeated declarations under one grouped selector. Jens built a tool to test it on 30 real sites and found it can still cut uncompressed file size, if applied selectively. Jens Oliver Meiert Local Visual Regression Testing for Agents with Playwright — A look at using Playwright's toHaveScreenshot matcher to give coding agents a consistent local visual-feedback loop. Paolo Ricciuti Building Interfaces That Understand What Users Want to Do — A look at using small AI 'decision models' to pick from options you define, including via Chrome's experimental, on-device Decisions API. Agustin Barrientos CSS-Tricks, Version 20 — Now under new ownership, the site is getting JavaScript cleanup, a Sass reorganization, and more, which Geoff explains in detail. Geoff Graham A Groundbreaking Upgrade to SVG is Approaching: Linked Parameters are Almost Here Roman Komarov Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible Eric Bailey Re-Implementing :nth-child() with Modern CSS Temani Afif 🧰 Tools, Code & Resources Britecharts 3.0: Ready-Made, Accessible D3 Charts — A long-awaited major release for this library of reusable D3 charts makes them accessible by default, with screen reader data tables and keyboard navigation. Also adds dark mode, TypeScript types, and a treemap. The docs are really good. Marcos Iglesias The “Export CSV” Button Shouldn’t Time Out — Exports scan every row in the range and slow as data grows. TimescaleDB keeps them fast. $1000 credit on Tiger Cloud . Tiger Data (creators of TimescaleDB) sponsor 🎨 This Hue Shall Pass: A Contrast Checker That Fixes Failing Color Pairs — Paste in a palette to get a grid of every foreground and background pairing, graded against WCAG AA or AAA. It doesn't just flag failures, you can also nudge near-misses into passing while keeping the hue intact. More background here . Clearleft Liquid Glass Forge: Refraction Behind Native HTML Controls — An experimental WebGL2 and CPU rendering engine for glass refraction, a la Apple's Liquid Glass. You can see a demo here . Nami Poursafargholi 🔡 Tinkerfont: A Font Inspection and Switching Tool for Chrome & Firefox — Install this extension and you get a quick way to inspect fonts on the current page (and their properties), and try alternative fonts directly on the page. Mighil BagUI: Components & Blocks for Building SaaS Landing Pages — A free collection that includes clean, customizable marketing pages, app pages, blocks, and templates for React and shadcn/ui users. Source code . Anelka Bagalane Master CSS 2.0: A Markup-Driven CSS Language — A utility-class framework where one class can carry a value, selector and condition (e.g. fg-blue-70:hover@sm ). v2 adds design tokens defined in your own CSS, a wide-gamut color palette, and linting and editor tooling. Aoyue Design 📰 Classifieds 🔁 Your agent checks web work with a refresh. On mobile it needs a device. Expo Simulators gives it one in the cloud. 📅 Booking forms without a backend : Real availability, live totals and deposits via your own Stripe or PayPal. CraftForms, from €6/month . ✍️ Foxit : Still redirecting users to a signing portal? 6 eSignature APIs compared on embedded signing, pricing and integration effort. 🛑 Finally, if you want to keep the bots out … A Blunt Banhammer Blocks Basic Bots Ballistically — Terence Eden's site was plagued by bots using up his bandwidth, so he built an interesting honeypot that lures the robots.txt -ignoring bots in and hands out a ban. It works, with an almost 90% drop in bandwidth used, but there are some tradeoffs. If you're happy to lean on the cloud for protection, Nick Gray recounts his year of fighting scrapers with Cloudflare , including his firewall rules and failed experiments. Meanwhile, with a more… 'creative' approach, Utku Sen filled a test site's code with taboo phrases and found AI agents refused to touch it . This may be more useful if you want to prevent casual reverse engineering/vulnerability hunting, though. Finally, even if you welcome crawlers, they can make your analytics misleading. Hugo Attal looked into his server logs and found 90% of his 'human' visitors were bots . Till next time…

items.titleJa: CSS Optimization: Is Using Declarations Just Once (UDJO) Still Effective Today?
items.summaryJa: UDJO（ declarations just once）は、古くからのDRY原則に基づくCSSの重複削減手法で、宣言の繰り返しをまとめてスタイルの保守性とファイルサイズの削減を目指す。著者は20サイト以上の検証を通じ、UDJOが必ずしもファイルサイズを削減するとは限らないケースがある一方で、適切なデータとツールを用いれば多くの場合でサイズ削減につながると結論づけている。つまり、UDJOは現代のCSS最適化において有効であり得る手法として、保守性とパフォーマンスの両方を念頭に導入すべきだと示唆している。

items.titleJa: 【CSSだけ】遷移時に共通の画像をシームレスに見せる

items.title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
items.summary: AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026 Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August , September , and October . November 2026 Summary In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July. OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one . OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December. More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on. Decision models account for 26% of all requests Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive. Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model. They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model. Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend. Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models. Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did. This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively. Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%. New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%. Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July. A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps: A voice model turns the user’s speech into text A language model writes the reply Another voice model reads the reply back to the user Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled. Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped. For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both. Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54. Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five. Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI. But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets. On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period. Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten. Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models. Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab. Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens. AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one. Also in October’s data Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two. Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten. OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0. About this data This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026. A few notes on measurement: Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ. Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month. Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list. Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025. Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens. Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day. A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month. All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated. Read more about our methodology , and explore or download the public data . items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 now available on AI Gateway
items.summary: Claude Fable 5.2 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway . Fable 5.2 is built for open-ended technical work and improves on earlier Fable models in coding, reasoning, and vision. It can run long, ambiguous tasks unattended, and works as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, or as an advisor that other Claude models consult on harder problems. It also communicates more clearly and generates output faster than earlier Fable models. Effort runs from low to max , with high as the API default. Fable 5.2 has cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Access to Claude Fable 5.2 requires data retention. Anthropic does not support Zero Data Retention for the model. Prompts and completions are retained for 30 days and are not used to train Claude. If your team has ZDR turned on, AI Gateway returns an error instead of sending the request to Fable 5.2. To keep requests served when a classifier is triggered, use model fallbacks . Add a models array to providerOptions.gateway , and AI Gateway tries each model in order when the cybersecurity classifier declines a request. Call it through the AI SDK , the Chat Completions , Responses , and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. Use anthropic/claude-fable-5.2 as the model name: This request falls back to Opus 5.5, then Sonnet 5.5, if the cybersecurity classifier declines it. The models option works the same way on every AI Gateway API format. To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup: Try Claude Fable 5.2 in the model playground . items.title: Muse Ember now available on AI Gateway
items.summary: Muse Ember from Meta is now available on AI Gateway . It is a lightweight reasoning model for the high-volume parts of an agent run, such as coding sub-tasks, tool calls, and document analysis. Muse Ember handles the bounded tasks agents repeat many times in a single run, like implementing a helper function, calling a tool, or summarizing a document. The model accepts text, image, and video input with a 1M-token context window, so an agent can pass it code, screenshots, documents, and clips in the same run. Tool calling lets your application feed each result into the next step. Reasoning effort is adjustable from minimal to max . Call it through the AI SDK , the Chat Completions , Responses , and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway.
